title: Creating a Simple Automated Status Check
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of creating a simple automated status check and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to creating a simple automated status check.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on creating a simple automated status check. A status-check workflow should perform an explicit check and return a meaningful non-zero exit code when the check fails. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Creating a Simple Automated Status Check matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. A status-check workflow should perform an explicit check and return a meaningful non-zero exit code when the check fails. Keep workflow files in `.github/workflows/`, name jobs and steps clearly, and verify a committed change from the Actions run page rather than assuming a saved YAML file executed.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: A status-check workflow should perform an explicit check and return a meaningful non-zero exit code when the check fails. Keep workflow files in `.github/workflows/`, name jobs and steps clearly, and verify a committed change from the Actions run page rather than assuming a saved YAML file executed. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Printing workflow information
items.text: Use `${{ ... }}` for workflow expressions and the correct context for the field. Treat event-derived values as data: pass untrusted text through an environment variable and quote it instead of inserting it into shell source.

content_blocks.expected_output: A push or pull request starts a read-only job; replace the demonstration command with a check appropriate to the repository.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a test repository or static validation first. Confirm the snippet matches the repository, runner, permissions, and current GitHub documentation.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Remove temporary test workflows and never carry test credentials or sample outputs into production.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to creating a simple automated status check. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain creating a simple automated status check, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Create and inspect the first workflow in a repository before adding complexity.

content.task: Apply creating a simple automated status check to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: A status-check workflow should perform an explicit check and return a meaningful non-zero exit code when the check fails.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: A status-check workflow should perform an explicit check and return a meaningful non-zero exit code when the check fails. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: A status-check workflow should perform an explicit check and return a meaningful non-zero exit code when the check fails.
Keep workflow files in `.github/workflows/`, name jobs and steps clearly, and verify a committed change from the Actions run page rather than assuming a saved YAML file executed.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
